Resolution and ratio Rendering at 200% of the final size and scaling down afterwards hides the jagged

chunks.headingPath: Final render settings › What breaks in the middle of the night
chunks.text:
What breaks in the middle of the night Leaving a render running with the disk nearly full. Blender writes each frame as 
it finishes, and when the space runs out it stops without warning and without 
saving the sequence ’ s progress.

Three-point lighting A scene with a single source looks flat. The classic arrangement fixes most of 
it before you touch a single material.

The three lights The key  is the main one, about 45 degrees off the object and a little above 
the eye line. It decides where the light comes from and where shadows land. The fill  sits opposite, at half or a third of the key ’ s strength. It is not 
there to remove the shadow — it is there so the shadow stops being black. The rim  comes from behind, pointing at the camera. That is what separates 
the object from the background and gives back the sense of volume.

The common mistake Turning the key up when the image looks dull. The problem is rarely a lack of 
light; it is a lack of contrast between the lit and the shadowed areas.

chunks.headingPath: Grid and alignment › When grid, when flex
chunks.text:
When grid, when flex Grid is for two dimensions, flex is for one. Writing flex-wrap  and working out 
widths by hand usually means grid was the answer.

chunks.headingPath: Grid and alignment › Columns that fit themselves
chunks.text:
Columns that fit themselves repeat(auto-fit, minmax(220px, 1fr))  makes as many columns as will fit, with 
no media query at all. It is the trick that saves the most CSS.

Spacing gap  rather than margins on the children. A margin on the last item leaves a 
space that someone will later try to remove with a special selector.

Moving around Jumping to a symbol ’ s definition and back without leaving the keyboard is what 
saves the most time in a large file.

chunks.headingPath: Editor shortcuts › Editing in several places
chunks.text:
Editing in several places Selecting every occurrence of a word and editing all three at once avoids the 
classic mistake: changing two and forgetting the third.

chunks.headingPath: Editor shortcuts › Searching the whole project
chunks.text:
Searching the whole project Search by regular expression with an extension filter. That is how to find where 
a constant came from when its name is too generic for a plain grep.

Borrowing and ownership The compiler is not being difficult — it is refusing a program that would fail 
at runtime in another language. Fighting the borrow checker is usually a sign 
that the design is what is wrong.

Errors Result  instead of exceptions changes how a function is written: the failing 
path is visible in the signature, so the caller cannot pretend it is not there.

Performance Measure before optimising. Speeding up a function worth 2% of the total changes 
nothing while the real bottleneck sits in an allocation inside a loop.

chunks.headingPath: Undoing things in Git › Not committed yet
chunks.text:
Not committed yet git restore <file>  throws the change away and there is no going back. 
git restore --staged <file>  only takes it out of staging and keeps the text — 
that is the one that serves most of the time.

chunks.headingPath: Undoing things in Git › Committed, not pushed
chunks.text:
Committed, not pushed git commit --amend  fixes the commit on top: wrong message, forgotten file. 
git reset --soft HEAD~1  takes the commit apart and puts everything back in 
staging, which helps when it bundled two things that should have been separate.

chunks.headingPath: Undoing things in Git › Already pushed
chunks.text:
Already pushed Now it is not erased, it is corrected on top. git revert <commit>  writes a new 
commit that undoes the old one, and the history keeps telling the truth. 
Rewriting what is already on the server breaks the clone of whoever pulled.

chunks.headingPath: Undoing things in Git › What gets forgotten
chunks.text:
What gets forgotten git reflog  keeps every place HEAD pointed over the last few days. A “ lost ” 
commit is almost never lost — it is there, unnamed, waiting.

chunks.headingPath: To read later › Persistent data structures
chunks.text:
Persistent data structures A structure that returns a new version instead of altering the old one. It is 
what makes undo free, and the idea behind most immutable state libraries.

Vector databases Storing meaning rather than words raises a new question: how to find the nearest 
neighbour without comparing against everything. HNSW is the answer that stuck.

chunks.headingPath: To read later › Typography on small screens
chunks.text:
Typography on small screens Almost everything known about leading and line length came from paper. Worth 
checking what still holds when the column is 320 pixels wide.

The starter Feed it equal weights of flour and water, always at the same hour. A healthy one 
doubles in four to six hours — if it takes twelve, it is weak and the loaf will 
come out heavy.

The dough Thirty minutes of autolyse before adding the salt. The flour takes up the water 
on its own in that time, and the dough turns silky with almost no kneading.

chunks.headingPath: Sourdough bread › Why mine came out dense
chunks.text:
Why mine came out dense Baking too early. The rise looked finished because the dough had grown, but the 
test is different: press it with a finger and watch how slowly the dent fills 
back. If it springs straight back, it is not ready.

chunks.headingPath: Focus and interruption › The cost of switching
chunks.text:
The cost of switching An interrupted task does not resume where it stopped. The mind holds a residue 
of the previous problem, and for a while you work on both at half capacity.

Batching Answering messages twice a day rather than as they arrive removes most of the 
switching without making anyone wait in any real sense.

chunks.headingPath: Focus and interruption › What actually helped
chunks.text:
What actually helped Writing down the next concrete step before stopping. Coming back to “ continue 
the refactor ”  costs ten minutes; coming back to “ extract the parser into its own 
module ”  costs nothing.

Line length Between 45 and 75 characters. Longer and the eye loses the start of the next 
line; shorter and the rhythm breaks every few words.

Vertical rhythm Line height around 1.5 for body text, tighter for headings. Large type needs 
proportionally less leading, which is why a heading set at the paragraph ’ s ratio 
always looks loose.

Contrast Grey text on white is a design decision that costs readability. If the copy 
matters it gets full contrast — the softness belongs to the labels around it.

# Final render settings

## Samples

Cycles at 128 samples with denoise on usually comes out clean. Past 256 the
gain is small and the time doubles.

## Resolution and ratio

Rendering at 200% of the final size and scaling down afterwards hides the jagged
edges better than any smoothing filter.

## What breaks in the middle of the night

Leaving a render running with the disk nearly full. Blender writes each frame as
it finishes, and when the space runs out it stops without warning and without
saving the sequence's progress.

blender/lighting.md.source:
# Three-point lighting

A scene with a single source looks flat. The classic arrangement fixes most of
it before you touch a single material.

## The three lights

The **key** is the main one, about 45 degrees off the object and a little above
the eye line. It decides where the light comes from and where shadows land.

The **fill** sits opposite, at half or a third of the key's strength. It is not
there to remove the shadow — it is there so the shadow stops being black.

The **rim** comes from behind, pointing at the camera. That is what separates
the object from the background and gives back the sense of volume.

## The common mistake

Turning the key up when the image looks dull. The problem is rarely a lack of
light; it is a lack of contrast between the lit and the shadowed areas.
blender/lighting.md.title: Three-point lighting

# Grid and alignment

## When grid, when flex

Grid is for two dimensions, flex is for one. Writing `flex-wrap` and working out
widths by hand usually means grid was the answer.

## Columns that fit themselves

`repeat(auto-fit, minmax(220px, 1fr))` makes as many columns as will fit, with
no media query at all. It is the trick that saves the most CSS.

## Spacing

`gap` rather than margins on the children. A margin on the last item leaves a
space that someone will later try to remove with a special selector.

# Editor shortcuts

## Moving around

Jumping to a symbol's definition and back without leaving the keyboard is what
saves the most time in a large file.

## Editing in several places

Selecting every occurrence of a word and editing all three at once avoids the
classic mistake: changing two and forgetting the third.

## Searching the whole project

Search by regular expression with an extension filter. That is how to find where
a constant came from when its name is too generic for a plain grep.

# Rust notes

## Borrowing and ownership

The compiler is not being difficult — it is refusing a program that would fail
at runtime in another language. Fighting the borrow checker is usually a sign
that the design is what is wrong.

## Errors

`Result` instead of exceptions changes how a function is written: the failing
path is visible in the signature, so the caller cannot pretend it is not there.

## Performance

Measure before optimising. Speeding up a function worth 2% of the total changes
nothing while the real bottleneck sits in an allocation inside a loop.

git/undoing.md.source:
# Undoing things in Git

## Not committed yet

`git restore <file>` throws the change away and there is no going back.
`git restore --staged <file>` only takes it out of staging and keeps the text —
that is the one that serves most of the time.

## Committed, not pushed

`git commit --amend` fixes the commit on top: wrong message, forgotten file.
`git reset --soft HEAD~1` takes the commit apart and puts everything back in
staging, which helps when it bundled two things that should have been separate.

## Already pushed

Now it is not erased, it is corrected on top. `git revert <commit>` writes a new
commit that undoes the old one, and the history keeps telling the truth.
Rewriting what is already on the server breaks the clone of whoever pulled.

## What gets forgotten

`git reflog` keeps every place HEAD pointed over the last few days. A "lost"
commit is almost never lost — it is there, unnamed, waiting.
git/undoing.md.title: Undoing things in Git

kitchen/sourdough.md.source:
# Sourdough bread

## The starter

Feed it equal weights of flour and water, always at the same hour. A healthy one
doubles in four to six hours — if it takes twelve, it is weak and the loaf will
come out heavy.

## The dough

Thirty minutes of autolyse before adding the salt. The flour takes up the water
on its own in that time, and the dough turns silky with almost no kneading.

## Why mine came out dense

Baking too early. The rise looked finished because the dough had grown, but the
test is different: press it with a finger and watch how slowly the dent fills
back. If it springs straight back, it is not ready.

# Typography notes

## Line length

Between 45 and 75 characters. Longer and the eye loses the start of the next
line; shorter and the rhythm breaks every few words.

## Vertical rhythm

Line height around 1.5 for body text, tighter for headings. Large type needs
proportionally less leading, which is why a heading set at the paragraph's ratio
always looks loose.

## Contrast

Grey text on white is a design decision that costs readability. If the copy
matters it gets full contrast — the softness belongs to the labels around it.
